title: Inference Cost Workshop: Quantization & Batching Hands-on Lab
content:
Purpose:
This hands-on workshop guide is designed for solutions engineers running a customer POC that demonstrates practical inference cost and latency improvements using quantization, batching, and lightweight KV/prefix caching. The goal is to give customers an executable lab they can run during a 90–120 minute workshop and leave with concrete numbers and reproducible artifacts.

Scope / Learning objectives:
- Measure baseline throughput/latency/cost for a medium-sized open model (e.g., 7B) on Redwood Hosted or a Dedicated test pool.
- Apply model quantization profiles (fp16 -> int8/GPTQ-style) and measure token-level cost delta.
- Configure continuous batching parameters (max_batch_tokens, max_latency_ms) and observe tradeoffs.
- Implement a simple prefix/KV cache for chat-like workloads and estimate hit-rate benefits.
- Produce a one-page findings summary for the customer.

Prereqs (attendee & environment):
- Laptop with Python 3.10+, Git, curl.
- Redwood account with test credits OR access to a Dedicated QA pool.
- Optional: Local Docker for running a lightweight sample client service.
- Repo: clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/se-labs (we'll use quant-batch-samples).

Estimated time: 90–120 minutes

Lab outline (high level):
1) Kickoff & baseline (20–30m)
   - Run sample throughput and per-token cost measurements against current model.
   - Capture metrics: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens.
2) Quick quantization pass (20–30m)
   - Apply a conservative quant profile (fp16 -> int8 8-bit symmetric) using the provided toolchain.
   - Re-run measurements and capture quality checks (sample prompts).
3) Batching exploration (20–25m)
   - Toggle batching configs: small-latency vs throughput-optimized.
   - Profile the composite effect with quantized model.
4) Prefix/KV caching demo (15–20m)
   - Demonstrate cache hits on repeated system prompts / shared prefixes.
5) Wrap & customer summary (10m)
   - Export numbers, quick slide with recommendations and next steps.

Detailed steps and commands:
Step 0 — Setup repo and virtualenv\n$ git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/se-labs.git
$ cd se-labs/quant-batch-samples
$ python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
$ pip install -r requirements.txt  # includes redwood-client, locust/bench harness

Step 1 — Baseline measurement (hosted test model)
- File: ./benchmarks/baseline_run.py (provided in repo)
- Quick curl example (hosted API):
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.inference/v1/generate \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"open-7b","input":"Write a concise summary of product requirements for a search feature.","max_tokens":150}' \n| jq .

- Run the local benchmark harness (single-client, 30s):
  python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model open-7b --duration 30 --concurrency 4 --out baseline.json

Record: p50/p95 latency, tokens_per_sec, server_side_cost_usd (if using Hosted return).

Step 2 — Quick quantization pass
- Use the repo script to produce an 8-bit quantized artifact (locally or via build cluster). This is a conservative lab flow — do NOT recommend aggressive per-customer without evals.
  python quantize/convert.py --model open-7b --mode int8 --out models/open-7b-int8/

- Deploy the quantized artifact to the test pool or reference a quantized variant provided in the Redwood model catalog (e.g., open-7b-int8).
- Re-run the benchmark:
  python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model open-7b-int8 --duration 30 --concurrency 4 --out quant_int8.json

- Quick quality check: pick 6 prompts (3 short, 3 long) from ./benchmarks/qa_prompts.txt and compare perplexity/semantic parity heuristics in ./benchmarks/compare_quality.py
  python benchmarks/compare_quality.py baseline.json quant_int8.json --prompts ./benchmarks/qa_prompts.txt

Expected observation: ~1.6–2.5x reduction in token compute cost on GPU for int8 vs fp16 for many kernel paths; small quality deltas on a subset of prompts.

Step 3 — Batching config exploration
- Concepts to highlight to customers: batch size (in tokens), max_latency_ms, dynamic vs fixed batching.
- Example server config snippet (as CLI-style key/value we use in the lab):
  --batch.max_tokens=4096 \
  --batch.max_latency_ms=12 \
  --batch.preferred_batch_size_tokens=1024

- Run three benchmark passes combining quantized model + batching presets:
  # low-latency preset
  python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model open-7b-int8 --duration 30 --concurrency 4 --batch-max-latency 6 --out batch_lowlat.json

  # balanced preset
  python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model open-7b-int8 --duration 30 --concurrency 8 --batch-max-latency 12 --out batch_balanced.json

  # throughput preset
  python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --model open-7b-int8 --duration 30 --concurrency 16 --batch-max-latency 30 --out batch_throughput.json

- Collect: tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, and per-token cost. Plot as three-line chart in the workshop slide.

Expected takeaway: batching + quantization compound — throughput improves substantially while small added latency can remain within customer SLOs for background/async workloads. For strict real-time interactive UX, tune max_latency_ms to 6–12ms.

Step 4 — Prefix/KV cache quick demo
- Provide a tiny Flask client that implements a simple in-memory KV cache for chat sessions. Key idea: if prefix tokens match a recent request, return cached KV (or cached partial logits) to eliminate re-encode cost.
- Pseudo-code (Python):
  from collections import OrderedDict
  class PrefixCache:
      def __init__(self, max_entries=200):
          self.store = OrderedDict()
          self.max_entries = max_entries
      def get(self, prefix_key):
          return self.store.get(prefix_key)
      def put(self, prefix_key, kv_blob):
          self.store[prefix_key] = kv_blob
          if len(self.store) > self.max_entries:
              self.store.popitem(last=False)

- Hook into the client loop to cache the model.kv_cache snapshot after the first token generation for a given prefix. On cache hit, send the minimal call (downstream runtime must support KV warm-start in the deployment).
- Run a synthetic workload with 50% repeated prefixes and measure RPS + token cost delta. Record cache hit-rate and effective cost reduction.

Troubleshooting / talking points:
- Quality regressions: show customers how to run a small eval set (50–200 prompts) and compute semantic similarity (embedding cosine) and token-level diffs.
- When quantization fails on edge cases, fallback to a slightly higher precision profile (e.g., Q4_0 -> Q5 or fp16).
- If batching increases p95 beyond acceptable, reduce max_latency_ms and/or use per-route latency SLO routing (demo slide explains routing to low-latency pool).
- Cache invalidation: discuss TTLs for session-specific data and policies for redaction when dealing with PII.

Deliverables for customer POC:
- benchmark results: baseline.json, quant_int8.json, batch_*.json (attach to confluence page)
- quality report: qa_summary.md (automatic export from compare_quality.py)
- short one-page recommendation slide: quantization suggestion, batching preset, cache hit-rate expectations, estimated monthly cost delta at X qps
- reproducible scripts and model references in GitHub repo branch: se-labs/<customer>-quant-poc

One-page summary template (for workshop final slide):
- Baseline tokens/sec: <value> | p95: <value> ms | estimated monthly cost: $<value>
- Post-quantization tokens/sec: <value> | delta: -<%> | quality delta: <notes>
- Best batching preset: <preset name> | throughput gain: <value>x | p95 impact: +<value> ms
- Cache hit rate used: <value>% | effective cost reduction: -<%>
- Recommended next steps: controlled canary with 5% traffic, run 2-week eval on user prompts, sign Dedicated sizing consult

Appendix: quick reference commands
- Compare two benchmark outputs and create a simple CSV:
  python benchmarks/compare_to_csv.py baseline.json quant_int8.json batch_balanced.json --out quick_results.csv

- Create a canary rollout plan (notes): use Redwood Console to create a route that pins 5% traffic to open-7b-int8 + batching-balanced, monitor token cost and user-facing latency, rollback on quality regressions. Link: https://console.redwood.ai/rollouts

Notes for SEs running the lab:
- Keep the workshop conversational: show numbers live but avoid aggressive promises.
- Save raw artifacts into the customer-specific branch; attach artifacts to the meeting notes.
- If customer uses private deployment, record needed infra: GPU type, network latency expectations, and KMS requirements for model artifacts.

References and further reading:
- internal quantization primer (Confluence link in linked_artifacts)
- sample code: https://github.com/redwood-inference/se-labs/tree/main/quant-batch-samples
- benchmarking script docs: ./benchmarks/README.md

Questions / TODOs for follow-up:
- Add a short section to the repo with instructions for ONNX export and a conservative fallback to fp16 when quality checks fail.
- Capture an example where int8 caused a coherence issue and document the mitigation.
- Create a Jupyter notebook that combines the benchmark results and generates the one-page slide automatically.

-- Miguel
(SE workshop draft)
